issues.legal_issue: An advocate’s failure to apply or account for client money entrusted for a specific purpose constitutes professional misconduct when established by reliable evidence.
material_facts: A client entrusted the advocate with money to complete a property purchase and discharge an outstanding mortgage.
The mortgage was not discharged, and the advocate did not account for the entrusted money.
The disciplinary tribunal and the High Court found that the advocate had not repaid the money he claimed to have given to an intermediary.
The Supreme Court found that a large body of reliable oral and documentary evidence supported the misconduct finding.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court’s order removing the advocate from its roll was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: An advocate must apply entrusted client money to the purpose for which it was given and account for it. The Court applied the Bar Councils Act and considered the findings of the Bar Council Tribunal and the High Court; it also referred to In the matter of an Advocate, Case No. XVI of 1942, and In re D. A. Shanmugasundaraswami, Misc. Case No. X of 1948, in discussing disciplinary action following High Court proceedings.

rule.if: professional_discipline_appeal and client_money_entrusted_for_specific_purpose and money_not_applied_to_that_purpose and money_not_accounted_for and reliable_evidence_supports_misconduct

predicates.professional_discipline_appeal: An advocate appealed a disciplinary decision concerning professional misconduct.
predicates.client_money_entrusted_for_specific_purp: A client entrusted money to an advocate for a specified purpose in carrying out the client’s matter.
predicates.money_not_applied_to_that_purpose: The advocate did not use the entrusted money for the purpose for which the client provided it.
predicates.money_not_accounted_for: The advocate did not account for the entrusted money to the client.
predicates.reliable_evidence_supports_misconduct: The disciplinary record contains reliable evidence supporting the finding that the advocate committed misconduct.

issues.definition: When an advocate’s disciplinary appeal concerns client money entrusted for a specific purpose, and reliable evidence shows the money was neither applied to that purpose nor accounted for, the High Court’s removal of the advocate from its roll is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: An objection that a professional-misconduct charge was imprecise or that the proceeding required proof beyond reasonable doubt does not defeat the finding where the charge caused no substantial prejudice and the evidence leaves no reasonable doubt about the misconduct.
material_facts: The advocate argued that the disciplinary inquiry was quasi-criminal, that the charge should have been more precise, and that the charge had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
The charge identified the money entrusted for discharging the mortgage, the alleged failure to use it for that purpose, and the failure to account for it.
The Supreme Court found no substantial prejudice or reasonable doubt as to the truth of the charges.
issues.conclusion: The objections to the charge and the standard of proof were rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the charge was not defective so as to mislead the advocate or cause substantial prejudice, and that the evidence left no room for reasonable doubt. It considered the disciplinary procedure under the Bar Councils Act.

rule.if: professional_misconduct_proceeding and charge_identifies_alleged_conduct and no_substantial_prejudice_from_charge and evidence_leaves_no_reasonable_doubt

predicates.professional_misconduct_proceeding: A disciplinary proceeding considers whether an advocate committed professional misconduct.
predicates.charge_identifies_alleged_conduct: The charge describes the conduct alleged to constitute the advocate’s misconduct.
predicates.no_substantial_prejudice_from_charge: The wording of the charge did not mislead the advocate or cause substantial prejudice to the defence.
predicates.evidence_leaves_no_reasonable_doubt: The evidence supporting the charge leaves no reasonable doubt about the alleged misconduct.

issues.definition: In a professional-misconduct proceeding, an objection to a charge identifying the alleged conduct is rejected when the charge caused no substantial prejudice and the evidence leaves no reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Findings that correspondence was altered or substituted should not support the misconduct decision when those allegations were not pursued before the disciplinary tribunal.
material_facts: The High Court found that certain letters had been interpolated or substituted.
The complainant’s counsel had not persisted before the tribunal in the allegations about the relevant alterations or substitution.
The Supreme Court left those allegations out of account and assessed the misconduct finding on the remaining evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court disregarded the findings concerning the alleged alterations and substitution, while finding sufficient independent evidence to sustain the misconduct decision.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the argument against relying on the correspondence allegations was well founded and excluded those allegations from its consideration of whether the charges were established.

predicates.professional_misconduct_appeal: An advocate appealed a decision in a professional-misconduct proceeding.
predicates.correspondence_alteration_allegations_no: The party alleging altered or substituted correspondence did not pursue those allegations before the disciplinary tribunal.

issues.definition: In a professional-misconduct appeal, findings about altered or substituted correspondence are disregarded when those allegations were not pursued before the tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary summons concerning an advocate already investigated by a High Court does not require a fresh evidentiary inquiry when the existing record and High Court findings are examined and the advocate receives a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The Supreme Court issued a summons after learning that the High Court had removed the advocate from its roll following an inquiry by a Bar Council Tribunal.
The Supreme Court examined the tribunal’s record and the High Court’s findings.
The advocate received notice and an opportunity to argue against disciplinary action.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court was not required to conduct a fresh inquiry by recording the evidence again.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order IV, rule 30 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, a High Court’s disciplinary order does not automatically dictate the Supreme Court’s order. The Supreme Court may generally examine the Bar Council Tribunal’s record and the High Court’s findings without starting a fresh inquiry, but must give the advocate a reasonable opportunity to be heard and may permit additional evidence where appropriate. The Court relied on In the matter of an Advocate, Case No. XVI of 1942; In re D. A. Shanmugasundaraswami, Misc. Case No. X of 1948; In the matter of Mr. 'G', a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court, (1955) 1 S.C.R. 490; and In the matter of 'D', an Advocate of the Supreme Court, (1955) 2 S.C.R. 1006.

predicates.supreme_court_disciplinary_summons: A disciplinary summons asks the Supreme Court to consider action against an advocate enrolled there.
predicates.prior_high_court_bar_council_inquiry: A High Court previously considered a disciplinary inquiry conducted by a Bar Council tribunal concerning the advocate.
predicates.tribunal_record_and_high_court_findings_: The Supreme Court examined the tribunal’s record and the High Court’s findings based on it.
predicates.advocate_given_reasonable_hearing_opport: The advocate had a reasonable opportunity to oppose the proposed action before the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court disciplinary summons follows a High Court and tribunal inquiry, the record and findings have been examined, and the advocate has had a reasonable opportunity to be heard, a fresh evidentiary inquiry is not required.

issues.legal_issue: An advocate found unfit by a High Court for a serious failure of integrity cannot remain enrolled as an advocate of the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The advocate was enrolled on the rolls of both the High Court and the Supreme Court.
The High Court found him guilty of grave professional misconduct and removed his name from its roll.
The Supreme Court found that the misconduct showed a failure to meet the high standard of integrity required of an advocate of the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court made the disciplinary rule absolute and removed the advocate’s name from its roll.
issues.legal_principle: Enrollment as an advocate of the Supreme Court is a privilege requiring a high standard of integrity. A High Court’s disciplinary order is not automatically followed, but a person found by the High Court to have fallen below the required standard is unfit to remain on the Supreme Court roll. The Court applied Order IV, rule 30 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, and relied on the disciplinary precedents discussed in its judgment.

predicates.supreme_court_advocate_disciplinary_proc: A disciplinary proceeding considers whether an advocate enrolled in the Supreme Court should remain on its roll.
predicates.high_court_removed_advocate_for_serious_: A High Court removed the advocate from its roll after finding serious professional misconduct.
predicates.high_court_found_integrity_below_require: The High Court found that the advocate’s conduct fell below the integrity standard required of an advocate.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court disciplinary proceeding concerns an advocate whom a High Court removed for serious misconduct and found below the required integrity standard, the advocate is removed from the Supreme Court roll.
